Reporting social media content
Platforms like Facebook/Meta or Twitter are receptive to taking down content when it falls within
three categories: 1) harmful content, 2) deceptive behavior, and 3) manipulative actors. However,
reported content may not be removed or may only be deprioritized if platform adjudicators
determine that it does not violate the terms of service.
•
Harmful Content: The content needs to demonstrate violations of the platform's community
standards. Hate speech, harassment, and calls for violence usually qualify. Facebook/Meta
has set up a "court" that they call "oversight board" to adjudicate incidents, meaning that it's
not necessarily a straightforward process.
•
Deceptive Behavior: If evidence is provided, most platforms will remove content / accounts
demonstrating what Facebook calls "coordinated inauthentic behavior" (e.g., troll farms or
bots) violating their terms of service.
Manipulative Actors: In some of USAID's more developed programs, partners, specifically
investigative journalists or think tanks doing online investigations are able to map out the bad
actors on social media platforms. They use the evidence to petition the platforms to get
'inauthentic" accounts taken down. Cases are not necessarily straightforward. For example,
public figures receive more leniency to remain online in spite of violations of terms of service.
For example, AID/Georgia's Information Integrity Program described the following actions to limit
harmful content:
1. Analyze online narratives and identify actors engaging in "coordinated inauthentic
behavior". The partner will share a list of accounts with Facebook/Meta who in turn will dig
deeper and ultimately take them down or de-promote content. While this work begins
"manually" there is technology that can identify patterns that reveal the source of harmful
content. It should be noted that online content may fall under different categories
(Fake/Manipulation/Out of Context) with different levels of response. Facebook/Meta also
works with trusted organizations such as the International Network of Fact-checking
Organizations (IFCN),Graphika or the Atlantic Council's digital forensics research lab to
do the leg work and flag activities through Facebook/Meta's user interface.
2. Support local fact-checking organizations to apply adequate standards and eventually
become part of IFCN and Facebook/Meta's fact checking program. Facebook/Meta's

Trusted Partners program allows vetted partners (e.g. local CSOs) to weigh in on content
takedown requests, and for example, make determinations on whether a takedown
request is legitimate.
3. Promote benchmarks on social media advertising policies. Facebook/Meta has increased
its standards in the U.S. especially after the recent U.S. elections' claims of the site's
vulnerabilities. The program is lobbying with Facebook/Meta to introduce the same
standards overseas, especially during elections.
The above description has focused on Facebook/Meta. Working with Google, YouTube, TikTok
or Twitter has been more difficult as they are behind the curve on controlling harmful content.
Nonetheless, addressing takedown requests is incredibly complex as company decisions are
informed by their business models and local and international laws on internet governance,
among other factors. For example:
• Reporting harmful content can be abused by malign entities seeking to discredit their
adversaries.
• Facebook/Meta has decentralized and very spread out "digital threats" teams making it
difficult to
react quickly. Facebook/Meta, for example, has different enforcement
capabilities depending on the market/jurisdiction - in places where they have a strong
market presence or interest in expanding, it employs a much more robust network of
content moderators, who are fluent in local languages, meaning the policy enforcement is
extremely uneven.
• In some instances, Facebook/Metachooses not to react for fear of being exposed for
housing malicious content.
• The rules are also subject to change. Recently, for example, Facebook/Meta changed its
policy to allow users from certain Eastern European countries to call for violence against
members of the Russian government and military. This is unprecedented and raises
serious concerns.
• The machine learning models and algorithms Facebook/Meta and other social media
companies use to verify harmful content is incredibly imperfect, to the point of oftentimes
being harmful. For example, it's not uncommon for posts about atrocities or hate speech
to get flagged by an algorithm as a violation of the terms of service and get taken down,
when they are in fact posted by a journalist or human rights organization to raise the issue.
• Even in places where Facebook/Meta has hired robust
and well-trained content
moderators, these moderators frequently find themselves subject to abuse, harassment,
and threats when content moderation decisions contradict government requests.
Additionally, there are new laws being proposed and enacted by various governments that
require social media platforms to hire local staff - what some civil society groups are
terming hostage-taking laws - that could further put local staff at risk.
Additional Resources
This section does not intend to offer an exhaustive list of all resources at USAID and State. It
simply offers a sample to begin the conversation with the experts.
